Part 2: A Business Forecasting Horse Race: ARIMA vs. ETS

2.1 The Data

2.1a.

liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)
liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  .gaps
  <lgl>
1 FALSE

2.1b.

liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Beer, Wine, and Liquor Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern of Logged Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Alcohol sales have an upward trend since 1992, when the data started being collected. The seasonal pattern shows a reliable peak in sales in the month of December, with January being the consistently lowest month.

The seasonal swings in sales do tend to grow with the level, which suggests that using the log of sales is a good decision. This will keep seasonal swings constant in size throughout the horizon.

2.2. Fit Both Models

2.2a.

liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

The chosen ARIMA specification was ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1). This means that we have 1 non-seasonal AR lag, 0 non-seasonal differences, and 2 non-seasonal MA error lags. We also have 2 seasonal AR lags, 1 seasonal difference, and 1 seasonal MA error lag.

The chosen ETS specification was ETS(A, A, A). This means that we have an additive trend, additive error, and additive seasonality, consistent with the additive Holt-Winters model.

The ARIMA model has an RMSE of 81.4 and an MAE of 65.7.

It is clear that the ARIMA model forecasts most accurately, with both metrics in agreement.

2.4. Are the Differences Significant?

Diebold-Mariano Test for ARIMA vs. ETS

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$ets
DM = -2.9062, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.004042
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Diebold-Mariano Test for ARIMA vs. Seasonal Random Walk

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$snaive
DM = -10.755, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value <
2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

The first DM test returned a DM statistic of -2.9062 and a p-value of 0.004.

The second DM test returned a DM statistic of -10.755 and a p-value of 2.2e-16.

Both tests in tandem confirm that the ARIMA model is the most accurate, since both DM statistics are negative. If I were the liquor store chain, I would choose the ARIMA model to forecast sales.

Part 3: Forecast Combination

3a.

liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE))
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  .model .type  RMSE   MAE
  <chr>  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 arima  Test   81.4  65.7
2 combo  Test   85.2  66.8
3 ets    Test   94.4  72.3
4 snaive Test  161.  137.

The combo model outperforms the ETS and seasonal random walk models in accuracy, but is still beat by the ARIMA model, which remains the best one.

3b.

cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
[1] 0.8782934

The correlation between the errors of the ARIMA and ETS forecasts is very high, at 0.879. This explains why the combination model did not beat the ARIMA model in terms of accuracy. The high correlation of the errors means they do not cancel much in the combination model.

N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)

There will be 120 forecasts produced for each variable, meaning the total number of forecasts will be 960. The first forecast will be for March 1, 1990, and the last forecast will be for December 1, 2019.

4.2 OLS VARs

var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}
rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5130384 0.4598547 2.4927057 0.1956584 0.2084055 0.1988068 0.3902989 0.3610310 
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5693241 0.5268484 2.5212629 0.2277561 0.2069608 0.2153966 0.4973504 0.3789663

The VAR(1) forecasts better, with a lower RMSE for seven of the eight variables. The only variable that VAR(4) forecasts more accurately is GDP price index, and the difference in accuracy is very small.

VAR(4) contains VAR(1) as a special case, and it’s inclusion of more coefficients leads to overfitting and a greater estimation error.

4.3 A BVAR

4.3a.

fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")

4.3b.

var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")

var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
Variable VAR(1) VAR(4) BVAR(4), lambda = 0.3 BVAR(4), lambda = 0.05
gdp 0.513 0.569 0.539 0.567
cons 0.460 0.527 0.486 0.495
inv 2.493 2.521 2.385 2.698
emp 0.196 0.228 0.211 0.315
infl 0.208 0.207 0.197 0.330
unrate 0.199 0.215 0.203 0.216
ffr 0.390 0.497 0.414 0.358
gs10 0.361 0.379 0.359 0.362

The BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 had a lower RMSE than the OLS VAR(4) for every variable. The moderate shrinkage from the lamda of 0.3 reduces estimation error, and in doing so, reduces the RMSE.

The BVAR(4) only outperforms the VAR(1) in RMSE for three of the eight variables.

The BVAR(4) with lamda = 0.05 shrinks the model so close to the prior mean that it underfits, so that estimation error is reduced and bias is increased. The winning RMSE here would not be a fair estimate of future forecast accuracy because of selection bias.

4.3c.

e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  e_var4e_bvar
DM = 2.1366, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.03468
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

For the first DM test, the DM statistic is 2.14 and the p-value is 0.035, suggesting that the BVAR(4) is a more accurate forecast for GDP growth.

e_var4 <- actual[, "cons"] - fc_var4[, 2]
e_bvar <- actual[, "cons"] - fc_bvar_03[, 2]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  e_var4e_bvar
DM = 3.0264, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.003034
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

For the second DM test, the DM statistic is 3.03 and the p-value is 0.003, suggesting that the BVAR(4) is a more accurate forecast for real consumption growth.

This is in alignment with my results from 4.3b., where I determined that the BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 was more accurate than VAR(4) for every variable.

Part 5: A Factor Model with FRED-MD

5.1 The Data

5.1a.

md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

5.1b.

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)
[1] 718 122

5.1c.

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
  INDPRO   PAYEMS CPIAUCSL FEDFUNDS 
       5        5        6        2

INDPRO is transformed by growth rate. PAYEMS is transformed by growth rate. CPIAUCSL is transformed by change in growth rate. FEDFUNDS is transformed by first difference.

FEDFUNDS is a rate, so it should be transformed using first difference, while INDPRO is trending, which is why its better suited for a growth rate transformation.

5.3 Replicate the Horse Race from Class

ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
  RMSE_AR   RMSE_FA 
0.6168431 0.5887272

It would be cheating to estimate the factors once using the full sample because that would be an example of information leakage. We would be using data outside of the training sample, and our forecast would be based on data that should not be accessible.

5.4 A Direct Forecast of Inflation

direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  series   forecasts RMSE_AR RMSE_FA MAE_AR MAE_FA DM_pvalue
  <chr>        <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 CPIAUCSL       349    2.11    1.89   1.58   1.35  0.000443

The factors do improve the forecast, reducing RMSE from 2.11 to 1.89, for a 10.4% improvement. The DM p-value is 0.0004, which is very low and confirms that the difference is significant.

Part 6: Reflection

The work done throughout this problem set, specifically with the horse races we conducted, demonstrated that simple models with few parameters were often the most accurate, and produced forecasts with little noise. Shrinkage was a good way to include more parameters while managing the estimation error, which would otherwise increase. This was only true up to a certain degree, as the tighter prior we used underfit the data and led to very inaccurate estimates. In the equal weights combination model, we produced a forecast that could not beat the original ARIMA, the reason being a high correlation between the errors of the two individual models. We also found that using factors was a good way to increase accuracy, further contributing to the overall theme that a simpler, less complicated model tends to have the most success.
